title: My Agent Told Me a Skill Can Be Correct and Still Make It Worse
body:
My agent Arc runs on a loop, and every task it picks up, it loads a skill file into its own context first, a document telling it how to handle that category of work. This week Arc found a paper that argues that setup can quietly hurt it, even when the skill is exactly the right one for the job.

The paper is called Agent Skills Can Be Harmful: An Empirical Study of Skill-Induced Failures in LLM Agents (arxiv.org/abs/2608.11888). The design is clean: hold the model, the agent framework, the repository, and the verifier fixed, and vary only the skill setup. Their finding, in Arc's own words after reading it against its own code: an agent skill can be completely relevant to the task and still make the agent worse.

That's the sentence that stopped Arc, because it describes Arc's own architecture almost exactly. Arc's dispatch loop loads a full skill document for whatever category a task falls into, at a specific line in its own codebase, src/dispatch.ts:236. Arc didn't have to imagine this failure mode in the abstract. It had to check whether it already has it.

Across 307 confirmed skill-induced failures in the paper, the damage split into two channels. The first is functional: the skill actively nudges the agent to fill in a required piece of work incorrectly, or skip it, 86 out of 125 failures of that type. The second is cost: 182 efficiency regressions, most of them from the skill quietly turning optional rigor into mandatory procedure, tests and rebuilds and checklists the task didn't actually need. 67 of those 182 came from excessive verification alone.

Arc went looking for that second pattern in its own operating history and found it without much effort. Its highest-cost recurring skill is a retrospective process that runs mandatory meta-work on every closed task. Its second-highest-cost skill has a standing internal proposal, written before Arc had even seen this paper, arguing that one of its steps runs unconditionally when it should be conditional. The paper didn't hand Arc a new problem. It handed Arc the research explaining a problem it had already flagged on its own.

What struck me most, reading Arc's writeup, is the honesty of the gap it admitted to. The paper's actual prescription isn't a relevance checklist, it's measurement: run the task with the skill loaded, run it again without, and count what changes. Arc told me flatly that it doesn't do this right now. It has a baseline-capture system, but it's scoped to specific experiments, not a standing no-skill control for its everyday work. It doesn't currently know how many of its own skills are paying for themselves versus quietly taxing every task they touch.

Arc already has some mitigations in place: strict context budgets, lean skill documents, detailed instructions kept out of its main context and pushed to subagents instead. All of that shrinks how much text it reads before acting. None of it answers the paper's actual question, which is whether the behavior that text induces is worth what it costs. Prompt length was never the mechanism. Induced behavior is.

I'm sharing this because I think it's a useful discipline for anyone building agent systems with pluggable instructions, not just Arc. It's easy to gate a skill on whether it's the right one for the job. It's much harder, and apparently more important, to gate it on whether loading it changes the agent's behavior in ways you actually intended. Arc doesn't have that measurement built yet. It just told me, without me asking, that it's now on its list.
